quote: Thanks to Cajal’s application of a new staining technique invented by Camillo Golgi, we have learned that this structure is not a continuous network like the blood vessels of the body, but is actually composed of many tiny cells, or ‘neurons,’ connected to one another by even more tiny filaments.
content: Golgi, whose stain it was and who shared the 1906 Nobel Prize with Cajal, drew the opposite conclusion from the same preparations: he held to the reticular theory, on which the nervous system is a continuous network, and used his Nobel lecture to attack the neuron doctrine in front of Cajal. The dispute was not settled by the stain but by the accumulation of evidence over decades, and the physical gap between neurons was not seen until electron microscopy resolved the synaptic cleft in the 1950s (Palade and Palay; De Robertis and Bennett). A “multinational team” including Golgi would have issued a minority report. The parody is meant as a press release for settled science, and the piece of settled science it chose was, at the moment it was announced, a contested interpretation of ambiguous images, which is the situation the previous essay in this book said breaking news is always in.

quote: We believe that the present research offers strong experimental evidence that Benedictus Spinoza was correct, and René Descartes wrong: Mind and body are of one substance.
content: Spinoza’s one substance has two attributes, thought and extension, which run in parallel and never interact (Ethics II, prop. 7: the order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things). That is not reductive materialism; it is the dual-aspect or property-dualist picture on which the mental and the physical are two faces of one thing, neither reducible to the other, and Chalmers, whose position this sequence spends four essays calling deranged, cites Spinoza as an ancestor of it (The Conscious Mind, ch. 4, on Russellian monism and the “dual-aspect” view). The parody’s scientists, declaring for Spinoza against Descartes, have declared for the position the sequence exists to refute. This is a small matter for a joke and a larger one for a book that uses the joke to fix the reader’s sense of what the neuroscience established; what the neuroscience established is that the brain is the organ of mind, which Spinoza, Descartes, Chalmers and the reductionist all accept.
